title: Lock-order graph analysis
description: Deadlocks need a lock-order cycle: thread A holds X wants Y while thread B holds Y wants X. Lock-order analysis builds the graph of lock acquisitions across the program; an acyclic graph means no deadlock is possible. Tools like Chord and RacerD check this statically, flagging the exact acquisition pair that closes a cycle.
method: Record lock acquisition order per path; build the global order graph; report cycles with the code locations forming them.
usage: Enforce a global lock order by convention; let the analyzer verify it; fix cycles by reordering acquisitions.

demo.code:
edges = [('A','X'), ('A','Y'), ('B','Y'), ('B','X')]
print('lock-order edges:', edges)
print('cycle X->Y->X detected -> DEADLOCK POSSIBLE (reorder B\'s acquisition)')

title: Session-type deadlock freedom
description: Session types don't just prevent miscommunication — well-typed session programs are deadlock-free by construction (for the structured fragment). The type system rules out the cyclic waits that cause deadlocks, so the proof comes free with typechecking.
method: Type channels with session types; the type system guarantees progress for well-typed closed programs; no separate analysis needed.
usage: Prefer session-typed concurrency where the protocol fits; get deadlock freedom as a typing corollary.

demo.code:
print('program session-typed, all channels dual')
print('type soundness corollary: DEADLOCK-FREE')

title: Choreographic programming
description: Choreographies describe the global interaction ('A sends x to B, then B sends y to C'); endpoint code is projected automatically. Projected programs are deadlock-free by construction — the global description can't express a cyclic wait, so the generated code can't have one.
method: Write the global choreography; project to endpoints; the projection theorem guarantees deadlock freedom.
usage: Use for multi-party protocols; the choreography is also the documentation.

demo.code:
print('choreography: A -> B: x; B -> C: y')
print('projected endpoints: deadlock-free by projection theorem')

title: Deadlock detection in databases (2PL)
description: Two-phase locking databases detect deadlocks via wait-for graphs over transactions and break them by aborting victims. The theory (deadlock detection vs prevention vs avoidance) is textbook, but the engineering — fast cycle detection on hot paths, victim selection minimizing wasted work — is what makes databases robust.
method: Build the transaction wait-for graph; detect cycles periodically or on wait; abort the victim (least work lost); retry.
usage: Keep transactions short (less deadlock surface); choose victim policies deliberately; monitor deadlock rates.

demo.code:
print('txn T1 waits for T2\'s row lock; T2 waits for T1\'s')
print('cycle -> abort T2 (younger), T1 proceeds, T2 retries')

title: Model-checked deadlock freedom
description: Model checkers verify deadlock freedom by exploring all reachable states and confirming none is a stuck non-terminal state. SPIN, TLC, and FDR check this routinely — 'no deadlock' is often the first property teams verify, because the checker needs no property beyond the definition of stuck.
method: Model the concurrent system; the checker flags states with no enabled actions that aren't valid terminal states; fix the design.
usage: Check deadlock freedom before any other property; a deadlocked design fails everything else too.

demo.code:
print('TLC: 2.1M states explored')
print('deadlock found: trace 9 steps -> design fixed -> re-check: CLEAN')

title: Lock elision and fine-grained splitting
description: The best deadlock analysis is needing fewer locks: lock splitting (one lock per independent structure), lock striping, and lock-free structures shrink the lock-order graph until cycles vanish. Design techniques that make deadlock analysis trivial by removing the locks.
method: Split coarse locks by independent data; stripe large arrays; replace contended locks with lock-free structures; re-run the analysis on the smaller graph.
usage: Design with fine-grained locking from the start; measure contention to find split candidates.

demo.code:
print('before: 1 global lock (serializes everything)')
print('after: 16 striped locks -> order graph trivially acyclic, 8x throughput')

title: Timeout-based deadlock avoidance
description: Try-lock with timeout turns potential deadlocks into retries: if a lock isn't acquired within T, release everything held and back off exponentially. Not a proof of freedom, but a pragmatic guarantee of progress — widely used where static ordering is impractical (e.g., locking two accounts in a transfer).
method: Use tryLock(timeout); on timeout release all held locks; exponential backoff with jitter; retry up to a limit; log contention.
usage: Use for ad-hoc locking (transfers, merges); tune timeouts from measured hold times; alert on repeated timeouts.

demo.code:
import random
random.seed(4)
ok = random.random() > 0.3
print('tryLock(db, 100ms):', 'ACQUIRED' if ok else 'TIMEOUT -> release all, backoff, retry')

title: Dijkstra's resource hierarchy
description: The oldest deadlock prevention: number all resources and require acquisition in increasing order. A cycle is then impossible by construction — you can't go down to close a loop. Simple, enforceable by code review or a one-pass checker, and still the backbone of kernel lock discipline.
method: Assign each lock a rank; enforce strictly-increasing acquisition; a static check or runtime assert verifies the order.
usage: Rank locks at design time; document the hierarchy; check it mechanically.
